title: Combining two bee colonies using the newspaper method
subtitle: The newspaper slows the merger to 24–48 hours, giving both colonies time to accept a shared scent before they meet.
excerpt: The newspaper method prevents the sudden fighting that kills bees when two colonies are merged without preparation. A single sheet of newspaper placed between the two sets of frames slows the merger: the bees chew through it over a day or two, and by the time they meet, they share enough hive scent to accept each other. Here is when to combine, which queen to keep, and how to set it up.
sourceNotes: NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), combining colonies section. BBKA Bee Craft technical notes on colony management. Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), Internet Archive, section on uniting swarms. British Beekeepers Association practical guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A colony that has lost its laying queen with no replacement developing. Without intervention, a queenless colony will decline to extinction over 4–6 weeks as existing bees die with no new brood to replace them.

A worker bee that has developed ovaries and begun laying unfertilised eggs in a queenless colony. Larvae from laying workers develop only into drones. A colony with laying workers is significantly harder to requeen or combine.

content.text: Two situations call for combining. The first is a colony going into autumn without enough bees to winter successfully on its own, usually a split that failed to build up, or a swarm that arrived late. The second is a
that has failed to raise a replacement queen. In both cases, combining with a healthy queenright colony is better than hoping the weak one recovers.

Keep the queen you prefer, the one from the stronger colony, the more productive one, the one with the calmer temperament. The other queen must be removed before combining, or she will be killed by the combined colony anyway, but in a way you cannot predict or control.

If one colony is queenless, the choice is made for you. If you want to replace both queens with a mated queen you have purchased, kill both existing queens, introduce the new queen in a cage on the queenless merged colony, and follow the standard queen introduction procedure.

Move the weaker hive to within 1 m of the stronger one. Move it gradually, 30 cm per day, if the hives are currently more than 3 m apart. Bees that have been flying to a fixed location need time to reorient, or a large proportion of the field bees from the moved hive will return to the old site.
Open the stronger (queenright) colony and smoke lightly. Remove the crown board.
Lay a single sheet of newspaper over the top of the frames. Pierce the newspaper 6-8 times with a drawing pin or the tip of the hive tool, this gives the bees a starting point to chew through.
Remove the floor and brood box from the weaker colony and lift it directly onto the newspaper. Do not shake or disturb the frames.
Replace the crown board and roof on top of the combined stack.
Leave the entrance reducer fitted and do not inspect for at least 48 hours. The bees chew through the newspaper in their own time; disturbing the hive before they have finished delays the process.

At the 48-hour check, the newspaper will be largely chewed away. Inspect gently and remove the remnants. Check that the queenright colony's queen is present and laying. Reduce the combined hive to one brood box by removing the least populated box over the following week.

attrs.cue: Fighting at the entrance 24 hours after combining
attrs.cause: The newspaper was removed or pierced too heavily, causing the bees to meet before scents merged, or both colonies still had queens
attrs.fix: Check both colonies for queens before combining. If fighting is already happening, a second layer of newspaper between the boxes slows the integration further.

attrs.cue: The weaker colony has laying workers
attrs.cause: It was queenless for too long before combining

The recommended approach for a laying-worker colony is to shake all the bees onto the ground 50 m from any hive, then let them find their own way back to a queenright colony. This sounds harsh but is the most reliable method; the field bees return to the nearest hive and the laying workers, which rarely fly, do not.
